newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU to be tougher on state aid - Van Miert.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU to be tougher on state aid - Van Miert.

text.p: European Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert, concerned about increased subsidies in the European Union, signalled on Wednesday he would try to be tougher in handling state aid cases.

Van Miert released provisional figures indicating that state support in the EU increased to at least 97 billion European currency units ($115 billion) on average per year in 1993-94 from 94 billion Ecus in the previous three years.
Subsidies increased especially in the two heavyweights Germany and France but also in Denmark and Ireland. Eight other EU countries had paid out less support to ailing sectors.
"We are concerned about it," Van Miert told a press conference, adding that there had been a development in the wrong direction.
"This is a lot more than the EU budget," Van Miert added. "Obviously we want to reduce state aid." He said public support could lead to unfair competition in the 15-nation EU.
Asked what he planned to do about it, Van Miert said: "Try to be even tougher than we have been."
He said the EU executive, which vets state aid to see that it does not harm competition in the EU, planned to put forward proposals in the coming months to "tighten the system."
"I hope we will get enough support to be able to do the job as it should be done," he added.
Van Miert also pointed out, however, that there had been only modest economic growth in 1993-94 while unemployment had risen, increasing domestic pressure to aid ailing industries.
In addition, there had been a special situation in Germany because of the amounts of support to the former communist half. In contrast, subsidies declined in western Germany.

Van Miert has come under increased pressure over the last year to clamp down on government subsidies, a campaign led mainly by smaller EU states which cannot match the vast amounts of money being pumped into industries by the bloc's big countries, notably Germany and France.

Companies not being helped are also reacting in horror to the record levels of aid flowing as a result of the unification of Germany, a greater exposure to international competition and the ongoing privatisation of loss-making firms.
The EU treaty bans any subsidies that distort fair competition, but leaves room for many exceptions. The most common is rescue and restructuring aid if limited to bringing a firm back to profit.
Van Miert said 42 percent of all public subsidies in the EU in 1993-94 had been paid out to industries, generating four percent of total value added.
Germany had paid out the largest amounts of state aid, 16 billion Ecus to industry. Italy came next with 11.7 billion Ecus and France third with industry subsidies of 6.8 billion.
In terms of percentage of value added generated by subsidies, Greece topped the list with 10.5 percent followed by Italy with 8.2 percent and Germany and France with 4.5 and 3.8 percent respectively.
Britain came last with only 0.8 percent of value added generated by state support, one tenth of the Italian figure.

Another reason for concern from the point of view of the functioning of the single market was that there had been increased aid to specific sectors. "This is a phenomenon that we are worried about," Van Miert said.
